tsh.name: TSH test
tsh.what: The single most sensitive blood test of thyroid function: TSH from the pituitary rises when the thyroid is underactive and falls when it is overactive, often before the thyroid hormones themselves leave their reference range. It is the first-line screening test and the value used to adjust levothyroxine.

measures.meaning: The pituitary's signal to the thyroid. High TSH means the pituitary is pushing a failing thyroid (hypothyroidism); very low TSH means it is being suppressed by excess thyroid hormone (hyperthyroidism). Laboratories add free T4 automatically when TSH is abnormal.

whyOrdered: Tiredness, weight change, feeling cold or hot, palpitations, anxiety, constipation or low mood
A goitre, neck lump or family history of thyroid disease
Atrial fibrillation, high cholesterol, depression, infertility or menstrual change
Monitoring levothyroxine (6-8 weeks after a dose change, then yearly) or antithyroid drugs
Before and during pregnancy in women with thyroid disease; on amiodarone or lithium
tsh.how: A venous blood sample at any time of day; people on levothyroxine usually take the dose after the sample.
tsh.preparation: None; tell the laboratory about biotin supplements, which can interfere with the assay and are paused for two days before the test.

interpretation.finding: High TSH with low free T4
interpretation.meaning: Primary hypothyroidism (the thyroid itself is failing)

interpretation.finding: High TSH with normal free T4
interpretation.meaning: Subclinical hypothyroidism: often repeated after three months; treatment considered if TSH stays above 10 mU/L or with symptoms, pregnancy or planning pregnancy

interpretation.finding: Low TSH with high free T4 or T3
interpretation.meaning: Hyperthyroidism: Graves disease, toxic nodules or thyroiditis

interpretation.finding: Low TSH with low free T4
interpretation.meaning: Pituitary (secondary) hypothyroidism, severe non-thyroidal illness or recent over-treatment; TSH alone cannot be trusted here

tsh.limitations: TSH is unreliable when the pituitary is diseased, during and shortly after severe illness ('sick euthyroid'), in the first trimester of pregnancy and with some medicines; it takes about six weeks to settle after a levothyroxine dose change, so testing sooner misleads. A normal TSH does not exclude thyroid problems that involve antibodies or nodules.

Pregnancy, older age, amiodarone, lithium, high-dose steroids and dopamine

Whether a nodule or goitre is present

ferritin.name: Ferritin test
ferritin.what: A blood test that estimates the body's iron stores by measuring ferritin, the protein that holds iron inside cells. It is the best single test for iron deficiency, the commonest cause of anaemia, and it also detects iron overload; because ferritin rises with inflammation, it is often read alongside CRP.

measures.meaning: Mirrors stored iron: low when stores are exhausted, high with iron overload but also with inflammation, infection, liver disease, alcohol and cancer.

whyOrdered: Anaemia, especially with small red cells (low MCV)
Tiredness, restless legs, hair loss or brittle nails where iron deficiency is suspected
Heavy periods, pregnancy, vegetarian or vegan diets, coeliac disease, after gastric surgery
Suspected haemochromatosis or iron overload from repeated transfusions
Monitoring iron treatment and, in chronic kidney disease and heart failure, iron status before intravenous iron
ferritin.how: A venous blood sample, often with a full blood count and sometimes transferrin saturation.
ferritin.preparation: None; a recent iron infusion or blood transfusion should be mentioned.

interpretation.finding: Ferritin below about 30 µg/L in an adult
interpretation.meaning: Iron stores are depleted (iron deficiency), whether or not anaemia is present yet; the cause, often blood loss, is then looked for

interpretation.finding: Normal ferritin with raised CRP and anaemia
interpretation.meaning: Inflammation may be masking iron deficiency; transferrin saturation or a trial of iron helps decide
Iron overload (haemochromatosis, transfusions) or severe inflammation, liver disease, cancer or a haemophagocytic syndrome
Stores are being replenished; treatment usually continues for months after haemoglobin normalises

ferritin.limitations: Ferritin is an acute-phase protein: any inflammation, infection, liver disease or alcohol excess raises it and can hide a deficiency. It does not show why iron is low; in adults iron deficiency is a reason to look for a source of blood loss, particularly in the gut.
ferritin.resultType: Numeric with a laboratory reference interval; a guideline cut-off defines depleted stores

quick.usedFor: Iron deficiency, anaemia, iron overload
quick.measures: Ferritin, the iron-storage protein, as a proxy for body iron stores

components.high: Inflammation, infection, liver disease, alcohol, iron overload, cancer
components.low: Iron deficiency from blood loss, poor intake, malabsorption or pregnancy

Liver disease, alcohol, obesity and metabolic syndrome
Recent iron infusion or transfusion
Time of day and assay differences between laboratories
cannotTell: Why iron is low (the source of blood loss must be sought separately)
Iron status reliably during active inflammation without other tests
Whether anaemia is due to something other than iron, such as B12 or folate deficiency
ferritin.medicinesNote: Oral and intravenous iron raise it; regular aspirin or NSAID use can cause the gut blood loss that lowers it; proton pump inhibitors reduce iron absorption.

creatinine-egfr.name: Creatinine and eGFR
creatinine-egfr.what: The everyday measure of how well the kidneys filter. Creatinine, a waste product of muscle, builds up in blood as filtration falls; the laboratory converts it, with age and sex, into an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), the number used to stage chronic kidney disease, detect acute kidney injury and adjust the doses of many medicines.

measures.meaning: Produced steadily by muscle and cleared by the glomeruli; rises when filtration falls, but only after a substantial loss of function
Millilitres of blood filtered per minute, estimated from creatinine by the CKD-EPI equation and adjusted to a standard body size; below 60 for three months defines chronic kidney disease

whyOrdered: Screening people with diabetes, high blood pressure or cardiovascular disease
Before starting or adjusting medicines cleared by the kidney (metformin, DOACs, many antibiotics) and before contrast scans
Swelling, reduced urine, tiredness, nausea or confusion
Acute illness, dehydration, vomiting or diarrhoea, particularly in people on ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics or NSAIDs
Monitoring chronic kidney disease, lithium and nephrotoxic drugs
creatinine-egfr.how: A venous blood sample; usually reported together with urea and electrolytes, and paired with a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio when kidney disease is being assessed.
creatinine-egfr.preparation: None; avoid a large meat meal and strenuous exercise the day before if the result matters for staging, and mention creatine supplements.

interpretation.finding: Creatinine rising over hours to days
interpretation.meaning: Acute kidney injury: dehydration, sepsis, obstruction or drugs; the eGFR is unreliable while the value is changing

interpretation.finding: eGFR below 60 on two tests at least 90 days apart
interpretation.meaning: Chronic kidney disease, staged G3a to G5 by the value and combined with the urine albumin category

interpretation.finding: eGFR 60-89 with no markers of kidney damage
interpretation.meaning: Not chronic kidney disease on its own; common with age

interpretation.finding: Small creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB
interpretation.meaning: Expected; a rise above about 30% prompts review of the dose and a search for renal artery narrowing

creatinine-egfr.limitations: Creatinine depends on muscle mass, so eGFR overestimates function in frail people and underestimates it in the very muscular; the equation assumes a steady state and is inaccurate in pregnancy, at extremes of body size and in rapidly changing illness. About half of kidney function can be lost before creatinine leaves the reference interval. Cystatin C offers a second estimate when the creatinine-based one is doubtful.

prothrombin-time-inr.name: Prothrombin time and INR
prothrombin-time-inr.canonicalName: Prothrombin time and international normalised ratio
prothrombin-time-inr.what: The prothrombin time measures how many seconds plasma takes to clot once the tissue-factor pathway is triggered; the INR expresses that time as a ratio standardised across laboratories. It is the test that tunes the dose of warfarin and one of the quickest measures of how well the liver is making clotting factors.

measures.meaning: Seconds to clot after tissue factor and calcium are added to citrated plasma; depends on factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen, the factors warfarin and liver disease reduce.
The PT expressed as a standardised ratio so that a result means the same whichever laboratory or reagent produced it; the number used to dose warfarin.

whyOrdered: Monitoring warfarin and deciding its dose
Assessing the liver's synthetic function in liver disease
Unexplained bleeding or bruising, and before surgery or a biopsy
Suspected vitamin K deficiency or disseminated intravascular coagulation
prothrombin-time-inr.how: A venous blood sample taken into a citrate (blue-top) tube, filled to the line so the anticoagulant-to-blood ratio is right; people on warfarin can use a fingerprick meter at home or in an anticoagulant clinic.
prothrombin-time-inr.preparation: None. Tell the laboratory or clinic about all medicines, supplements and any recent change in diet, illness or alcohol intake, which change the result.

interpretation.finding: INR within the target range set for the person on warfarin
interpretation.meaning: The dose is giving the intended degree of anticoagulation; the target depends on why warfarin is taken
Anticoagulation is stronger than intended and bleeding risk rises; the dose is reviewed, and a very high INR or bleeding is treated urgently
Anticoagulation is weaker than intended; a missed dose, a new medicine or a change in diet is looked for

interpretation.finding: Prolonged PT in someone not taking warfarin
interpretation.meaning: May reflect liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, a clotting-factor deficiency or disseminated intravascular coagulation, interpreted with the aPTT and other tests

prothrombin-time-inr.rangeNote: For someone taking warfarin the INR is read against the individual target range their prescriber has set, not against a population reference interval. In people not on anticoagulants the prothrombin time is read against the laboratory's own reference interval, which depends on the reagent used.
factors: Warfarin dose, missed doses and how consistently it is taken
Vitamin K intake (green leafy vegetables) and supplements
Antibiotics, antifungals, amiodarone, some antiepileptics and many other interacting medicines
Acute illness, diarrhoea, alcohol binges and liver disease
An under-filled citrate tube, which prolongs the result artificially
cannotTell: How well a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) is working: the INR is not calibrated for them
Whether bleeding will happen at a given INR, which also depends on age, other medicines and the reason for anticoagulation
Platelet problems, which need a platelet count and function tests
prothrombin-time-inr.limitations: The INR is only meaningful for vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin; direct oral anticoagulants prolong it unpredictably and need different tests. The prothrombin time depends on the reagent and is standardised only through the INR calculation.
prothrombin-time-inr.medicinesNote: Warfarin is the medicine the test monitors; many antibiotics, antifungals, amiodarone, NSAIDs and alcohol raise the INR, while rifampicin, carbamazepine and large amounts of vitamin K lower it.

iron-studies.name: Iron studies
iron-studies.what: A group of blood tests that together describe how much iron the body has stored, how much is circulating and how much of the transport protein transferrin is carrying it. Ferritin reflects the stores, serum iron and transferrin saturation the supply in transit, and the pattern across them separates iron deficiency from the anaemia of chronic disease and from iron overload.

components.name: Ferritin
components.measures: The storage form of iron; the single most useful marker of iron deficiency
components.high: Iron overload, inflammation, infection, liver disease, some cancers

components.name: Serum iron
components.measures: Iron circulating bound to transferrin at the moment of the sample
components.high: Iron overload, recent iron tablets, haemolysis
components.low: Iron deficiency, inflammation, chronic disease; varies through the day

components.name: Total iron-binding capacity
components.measures: How much iron the blood's transferrin could carry, an indirect measure of transferrin
components.high: Iron deficiency (the body makes more transferrin), pregnancy, oestrogen
components.low: Inflammation, malnutrition, liver disease, iron overload

components.name: Transferrin saturation
components.measures: The percentage of transferrin's iron-binding sites occupied, calculated from serum iron and TIBC
components.high: Iron overload including haemochromatosis

whyOrdered: Anaemia, especially with small red cells (a low MCV)
Tiredness, restless legs, hair loss or brittle nails when iron deficiency is suspected
Suspected iron overload or haemochromatosis
Monitoring iron treatment or blood transfusions
Assessing iron status in kidney disease, heart failure and before surgery
iron-studies.how: A venous blood sample, ideally in the morning because serum iron varies through the day.
iron-studies.preparation: Fasting is sometimes requested. Iron tablets taken in the previous 24 hours raise the serum iron, so the laboratory may ask for them to be paused; say if you have had an iron infusion or transfusion recently.

interpretation.meaning: Iron deficiency; the cause (blood loss, poor intake or absorption, pregnancy) is then looked for

interpretation.finding: Low serum iron and transferrin saturation with normal or high ferritin
interpretation.meaning: Usually the anaemia of inflammation or chronic disease, in which iron is present but locked away; ferritin alone can mislead here

interpretation.finding: High transferrin saturation and high ferritin
interpretation.meaning: Possible iron overload; genetic testing for haemochromatosis may follow
Iron is not the explanation; B12, folate, kidney function, thalassaemia and other causes are considered

iron-studies.rangeNote: Each component is read against the interval supplied by the laboratory that ran the test. Ferritin behaves as an acute-phase protein, so a value in the reference interval does not exclude iron deficiency when inflammation is present.
factors: Inflammation, infection and liver disease, which raise ferritin whatever the iron stores
Time of day and recent meals or iron tablets, which change serum iron
Pregnancy and oestrogen-containing medicines, which raise transferrin
Recent transfusion or intravenous iron
cannotTell: The cause of iron deficiency: bleeding from the gut, heavy periods, diet and malabsorption need their own investigation
Whether anaemia is present, which is a haemoglobin question
Iron status with certainty during active inflammation, when ferritin is unreliable
iron-studies.limitations: No single component is definitive: ferritin rises with inflammation, serum iron swings through the day and with meals, and the pattern across the panel is what the clinician reads. Soluble transferrin receptor is used in some laboratories to separate iron deficiency from inflammation.
iron-studies.medicinesNote: Oral and intravenous iron raise the results; proton-pump inhibitors reduce iron absorption over time; oestrogens raise transferrin.

quick.sample: Blood from a vein, ideally in the morning
quick.usedFor: Investigating anaemia and iron deficiency, suspected iron overload, monitoring iron treatment
quick.measures: Ferritin, serum iron, total iron-binding capacity and transferrin saturation

iron-studies.resultType: Numeric panel read as a pattern

vitamin-b12-folate.name: Vitamin B12 and folate
vitamin-b12-folate.what: Two blood tests, usually ordered together, for the vitamins the bone marrow needs to make normal red cells and the nervous system needs to keep nerves working. Deficiency of either causes anaemia with large red cells; vitamin B12 deficiency can also damage nerves, sometimes before the blood count changes.

measures.meaning: The vitamin absorbed in the last part of the small intestine with the help of intrinsic factor from the stomach; low in pernicious anaemia, after gut surgery, in strict vegan diets and with some medicines.
The B vitamin from green vegetables and fortified foods; low with poor diet, alcohol excess, pregnancy, malabsorption and some medicines.

whyOrdered: Anaemia with large red cells (a high MCV)
Numbness, tingling, balance problems or memory change that could be B12 deficiency
Tiredness, a sore tongue or mouth ulcers
Long-term metformin or acid-suppressing treatment, which can lower B12
Before and during pregnancy planning, for folate
vitamin-b12-folate.preparation: None usually; the laboratory may ask for a fasting sample. Say if you take B12 or folic acid supplements, or have had a B12 injection, which mask deficiency.

interpretation.meaning: Deficiency, whose cause (pernicious anaemia, diet, absorption, medicines) is then sought; further tests such as intrinsic-factor antibodies may follow
An indeterminate zone in which symptoms, the blood count and sometimes additional markers decide whether treatment is given
Deficiency from diet, alcohol, malabsorption, pregnancy or a medicine; treated after B12 status is known, because folic acid alone can worsen the nerve damage of untreated B12 deficiency

interpretation.finding: Both normal with a high MCV
interpretation.meaning: Other causes of large red cells are considered: alcohol, liver disease, thyroid disease, some medicines, bone-marrow disorders

vitamin-b12-folate.rangeNote: Both vitamins are read against the interval supplied by the laboratory that ran the test; assays differ, and a borderline B12 result is interpreted with symptoms and the blood count rather than as a fixed cut-off.
factors: Supplements, injections and fortified foods, which raise the results
Metformin, proton-pump inhibitors and H2 blockers, which lower B12 over years
Pregnancy and oral contraceptives, which lower measured B12
Recent meals, which raise serum folate
Liver disease and some blood disorders, which raise B12 without reflecting stores
cannotTell: Whether nerve damage from B12 deficiency will recover
The cause of a low result without further tests
Tissue B12 status precisely: the blood level is an imperfect proxy
vitamin-b12-folate.limitations: Serum B12 has a wide indeterminate range and can be falsely normal in people with intrinsic-factor antibodies; serum folate reflects recent intake more than stores. Treatment is often started on clinical grounds when a result is borderline.
vitamin-b12-folate.medicinesNote: Metformin, proton-pump inhibitors, H2 blockers and colchicine can lower B12; methotrexate, some antiepileptics and trimethoprim interfere with folate.

quick.usedFor: Investigating anaemia with large red cells, nerve symptoms, and monitoring people on long-term metformin
quick.measures: The blood levels of vitamin B12 and folate

vitamin-b12-folate.resultType: Numeric, read against the laboratory's intervals with a borderline zone for B12

components.measures: Serum cobalamin
components.high: Supplements, liver disease

vitamin-d.name: Vitamin D test
vitamin-d.what: Measures 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the storage form the liver makes from vitamin D obtained from sunlight on skin and from food or supplements. It is the best single measure of vitamin D status and is used when bone pain, muscle weakness, osteoporosis, malabsorption or a low calcium make deficiency likely.

measures.meaning: The circulating storage form, reflecting weeks of sun exposure and intake; the kidney converts it to the active hormone that raises calcium absorption.

whyOrdered: Bone pain, muscle weakness or unexplained fatigue when deficiency is suspected
Osteoporosis, fractures and before starting bone treatments
Low calcium or a raised alkaline phosphatase or parathyroid hormone
Conditions that impair absorption: coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, after bariatric surgery
Chronic kidney disease and some other long-term conditions

interpretation.meaning: Levels at which bone softening (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults) becomes likely; treatment with vitamin D is usually given
Below the level considered adequate for bone health; supplementation is often advised, particularly in groups at risk
Sufficient for bone health in most people
Usually from excess supplements; can cause a high calcium and is reviewed

vitamin-d.rangeNote: Vitamin D is read against widely used cut-offs for deficiency, insufficiency and adequacy that differ slightly between countries and professional bodies, not against a population reference interval. The laboratory reports the cut-offs it applies, and the assay method affects the value.
factors: Season and latitude: levels fall in winter and in people who cover their skin or stay indoors
Skin pigmentation, age and body weight
Supplements and fortified foods
Liver and kidney disease, which affect the conversion of vitamin D
The assay method, which changes results between laboratories
cannotTell: Bone density, which needs a DXA scan
Whether symptoms are caused by the deficiency, which is common and often coincidental
The active hormone level (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), a separate test used only in specific disorders
vitamin-d.limitations: Population screening is not recommended; the test is for people with symptoms or risk factors. Assays vary and the value moves with the seasons, so a single result is interpreted with the time of year and the person's circumstances.
vitamin-d.medicinesNote: Vitamin D supplements raise it; some antiepileptics, glucocorticoids, orlistat and cholestyramine lower it.

quick.usedFor: Suspected vitamin D deficiency, bone disease, malabsorption, before bone treatments
quick.measures: 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the storage form of vitamin D

vitamin-d.resultType: Numeric, read against deficiency and adequacy cut-offs

components.measures: The storage form of vitamin D
components.high: Excess supplements
components.low: Little sunlight, low intake, malabsorption, kidney or liver disease

hepatitis-b-serology.name: Hepatitis B tests
hepatitis-b-serology.what: A set of blood tests that shows whether someone has hepatitis B now, had it in the past, is immune from vaccination, or carries the virus long term. Each marker answers a different question: the surface antigen shows current infection, the antibodies show immunity or past exposure, and the viral DNA measures how actively the virus is multiplying.

measures.meaning: Part of the virus's outer coat; present in acute and chronic infection. Persisting beyond six months defines chronic hepatitis B.
The protective antibody; present after vaccination or recovered infection.
Marks exposure to the virus at some time; absent after vaccination alone. The IgM form points to recent infection.

measures.item: e antigen and e antibody (HBeAg, anti-HBe)
measures.meaning: Indicate how actively the virus is replicating in chronic infection.
The amount of virus in the blood, measured by PCR; guides the decision to treat and shows whether treatment is working.

whyOrdered: Abnormal liver tests or symptoms of hepatitis
Screening in pregnancy, before immunosuppressive treatment, and in people at higher risk
After a possible exposure, such as a needlestick injury
Checking immunity after vaccination
Monitoring chronic hepatitis B and its treatment
hepatitis-b-serology.how: A venous blood sample; the laboratory runs the markers as a panel and adds viral DNA when the surface antigen is positive.

interpretation.meaning: Current infection, acute or chronic; further markers and liver assessment follow, and specialist care is arranged
Immunity from vaccination

interpretation.finding: anti-HBs and anti-HBc positive, HBsAg negative
interpretation.meaning: Past infection that has resolved, with immunity

interpretation.finding: HBsAg positive for more than six months
interpretation.meaning: Chronic hepatitis B; the viral load, e-antigen status and liver tests decide on monitoring and antiviral treatment
Never infected and not immune; vaccination is considered

hepatitis-b-serology.rangeNote: Antigen and antibody results are reported as positive or negative (with a level for anti-HBs after vaccination); the viral load is a number whose meaning depends on the clinical context and the treatment guidelines in use, not on a reference interval.
factors: Timing after exposure: markers appear in sequence over weeks
Recent vaccination, which produces anti-HBs only
Immunosuppression, which can reactivate a resolved infection
Very early or 'window period' infection, when only anti-HBc IgM may be positive
cannotTell: How much liver damage has occurred, which needs liver tests, elastography or biopsy
Whether hepatitis C, D or other liver diseases are also present without their own tests
Exactly when the infection was acquired
hepatitis-b-serology.limitations: The markers must be read as a pattern; a single result can mislead in the window period, after vaccination or in people with weak immunity. Chronic infection needs long-term specialist monitoring even when the person feels well.
hepatitis-b-serology.medicinesNote: Antiviral treatment for hepatitis B lowers the viral load; the test monitors that treatment. Immunosuppressive medicines can reactivate the virus, so screening is done before they are started.

quick.usedFor: Diagnosing and monitoring hepatitis B, checking immunity, screening in pregnancy and before immunosuppression
quick.measures: Hepatitis B antigens, antibodies and viral DNA

hepatitis-b-serology.resultType: Positive or negative markers read as a pattern, plus a viral load

hiv-test.name: HIV test
hiv-test.what: A blood test that looks for the human immunodeficiency virus, usually by detecting both a viral protein (p24 antigen) and the antibodies the immune system makes against the virus. Modern combined tests become positive within a few weeks of infection; a positive screening result is always confirmed with a second test before a diagnosis is given.

measures.item: HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies with p24 antigen
measures.meaning: The standard fourth-generation laboratory screen, reliable from about 45 days after exposure; antigen detection shortens the window.
Fingerprick or saliva tests with results in minutes; a reactive result must be confirmed by a laboratory.

measures.item: HIV RNA (viral load) and CD4 count
measures.meaning: After diagnosis: the amount of virus and the number of CD4 immune cells, used to plan and monitor treatment rather than to screen.

whyOrdered: Routine screening: HIV testing is offered widely because early treatment protects health and prevents transmission
After a possible exposure, at the right interval
Symptoms of seroconversion or of an immune system under attack
Pregnancy screening, before some treatments and in people diagnosed with other sexually transmitted infections
hiv-test.how: A venous blood sample in a laboratory, a fingerprick rapid test in a clinic or pharmacy, or a home self-test kit.
hiv-test.preparation: None. The window period matters: a test taken too soon after exposure can be negative, so a repeat at the recommended interval may be advised.

interpretation.meaning: HIV infection is very unlikely; repeat testing is advised after any further exposure
Possible infection; a confirmatory laboratory test on a new sample is done before any diagnosis
HIV infection; referral to specialist care, where viral load and CD4 count guide antiretroviral treatment that keeps the virus suppressed
Inconclusive; the test is repeated at the interval recommended for the type of test used

hiv-test.rangeNote: Screening results are reported as negative or reactive, and confirmed positive or negative; no numeric reference interval applies. Viral load and CD4 count after diagnosis are numbers interpreted against treatment guidelines.
factors: The interval since exposure (window period), which depends on the test type
Post-exposure or pre-exposure prophylaxis medicines, which can delay antibody development
Rare false-reactive screening results, which is why confirmation is required
cannotTell: Whether infection occurred within the last few weeks, before markers appear
The stage of infection or the state of the immune system, which need the viral load and CD4 count
Other sexually transmitted infections, which have their own tests
hiv-test.limitations: No test detects infection immediately after exposure; results are only interpreted in relation to the timing of exposure, and a screening result is never a diagnosis on its own. Self-tests carry the same window-period limits and need confirmation.
hiv-test.medicinesNote: Antiretroviral prophylaxis can delay or blunt antibody responses; antiretroviral treatment lowers the viral load, which the monitoring tests track.

quick.type: Blood test (serology; rapid and self-tests available)
quick.sample: Blood from a vein, a fingerprick, or saliva for self-tests
quick.usedFor: Screening for HIV, testing after exposure, monitoring treatment once diagnosed
quick.measures: HIV antibodies and p24 antigen; viral load and CD4 count after diagnosis

hiv-test.specimen: Venous blood (serum) in the laboratory; capillary blood or oral fluid for rapid and self-tests
hiv-test.resultType: Negative, reactive or confirmed positive; numeric viral load and CD4 count in monitoring

blood-pressure-measurement.name: Blood pressure measurement
blood-pressure-measurement.what: The pressure of blood against the artery walls, recorded as two numbers: the systolic pressure when the heart contracts and the diastolic pressure between beats. Measured with a cuff on the upper arm, it is the most frequently taken measurement in medicine because raised blood pressure usually causes no symptoms yet drives heart attacks, strokes and kidney disease.

measures.meaning: The peak pressure as the left ventricle ejects blood, in mmHg.
The lowest pressure, while the heart refills, in mmHg.
Readings taken automatically over 24 hours by a worn cuff; the daytime average is the reference measurement for diagnosing hypertension.
Twice-daily readings taken by the person over several days with a validated arm cuff, averaged.

whyOrdered: Routine health checks and screening for hypertension
Confirming a raised clinic reading with ambulatory or home monitoring
Monitoring blood-pressure treatment
Dizziness on standing, when lying and standing readings are compared
In pregnancy, kidney disease, diabetes and after a stroke or heart attack
blood-pressure-measurement.how: Seated and rested for a few minutes, arm supported at heart level, a correctly sized cuff on the upper arm; readings are repeated and the average used. Ambulatory monitoring uses an automatic cuff worn for 24 hours; home monitoring uses a validated upper-arm device morning and evening for several days.
blood-pressure-measurement.preparation: Avoid caffeine, smoking and exercise for 30 minutes before; empty the bladder; sit quietly with the back supported and legs uncrossed; do not talk during the reading.

interpretation.meaning: Hypertension is suspected but not diagnosed: ambulatory or home monitoring confirms it, because clinic readings are often higher than usual (white-coat effect)

interpretation.finding: Ambulatory or home average above the diagnostic threshold
interpretation.meaning: Hypertension; the stage, cardiovascular risk and any organ damage guide lifestyle advice and treatment
Severe hypertension or an emergency; assessed the same day
Postural (orthostatic) hypotension, a common cause of dizziness and falls, often from medicines or dehydration

blood-pressure-measurement.rangeNote: Blood pressure is read against guideline thresholds for diagnosis and treatment targets, which differ between clinic, ambulatory and home readings and between countries' guidelines; it is not read against a laboratory reference interval.

thresholds.name: Clinic blood pressure suggesting hypertension
thresholds.context: A clinic reading at or above this prompts ambulatory (or home) monitoring to confirm the diagnosis

thresholds.name: Ambulatory or home average confirming stage 1 hypertension
thresholds.context: Diagnosis of stage 1 hypertension when the clinic reading is 140/90 or higher

thresholds.name: Stage 2 hypertension
thresholds.context: Treatment is offered to adults of any age with stage 2 hypertension

factors: Cuff size, arm position, talking, a full bladder and recent caffeine, smoking or exercise
The clinic setting itself (white-coat effect) and, conversely, masked hypertension that is normal in clinic but raised at home
Pain, anxiety, cold and the time of day
Medicines: decongestants, NSAIDs, steroids, oral contraceptives and stimulants raise it; antihypertensives, some antidepressants and alcohol change it
cannotTell: Whether arteries or organs have been damaged, which needs blood tests, urine tests, an ECG and sometimes imaging
The cause of high blood pressure, which is usually not identifiable and occasionally due to kidney, adrenal or other disease
Blood pressure inside the heart or lungs, which needs catheter studies
blood-pressure-measurement.limitations: A single reading is a poor guide: blood pressure varies minute to minute, and diagnosis rests on averaged out-of-clinic readings. Wrist and finger devices are less reliable than validated upper-arm cuffs, and irregular rhythms such as atrial fibrillation make automatic devices inaccurate.
blood-pressure-measurement.medicinesNote: Antihypertensive medicines are what the measurement monitors; NSAIDs, decongestants, corticosteroids and some antidepressants can raise it.

quick.sample: None: a cuff on the upper arm
quick.usedFor: Screening for and diagnosing hypertension, monitoring treatment, assessing dizziness on standing
quick.measures: Systolic and diastolic arterial pressure in mmHg

cervical-screening.name: Cervical screening (smear test)
cervical-screening.what: A sample of cells brushed from the transformation zone of the cervix, the band where the columnar lining of the cervical canal has been replaced by squamous cells and where nearly all cervical cell changes begin, taken with a small soft brush passed through a speculum. In England the sample is tested first for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), the virus behind almost all cervical cancer, and the cells are examined under the microscope only if that virus is found. Screening looks for the risk of cancer developing rather than for cancer itself, and it is offered to everyone with a cervix, including trans men and non-binary people.

measures.meaning: The virus types that cause cervical cancer, chiefly types 16 and 18. A negative result means the chance of cancer developing before the next screen is very low.
Looked at only when high-risk HPV is found. Cells are reported as normal, borderline, or as low-grade or high-grade dyskaryosis, according to how abnormal they appear.
A sample with too few cells, or obscured by blood or inflammation, is reported as inadequate and has to be repeated.

whyOrdered: Routine screening for everyone with a cervix aged 25 to 64 in England, at intervals that depend on age, the previous result and the programme (the four UK nations differ)
A repeat a year after a high-risk HPV result with normal cells, to see whether the infection has cleared
Follow-up after treatment of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), as a test of cure
Trans men and non-binary people who have a cervix: those registered with a GP as male are not sent automatic invitations and need to ask for screening
Not for investigating symptoms: bleeding between periods, after sex or after the menopause needs an examination of the cervix and referral, not a screening test
cervical-screening.how: A speculum is passed into the vagina so that the cervix can be seen, and a small soft brush is rotated in the opening of the cervix for a few seconds. The tip of the brush is put into a pot of preservative liquid and sent to the laboratory (liquid-based cytology). The appointment takes a few minutes and is usually done by a practice nurse.
cervical-screening.preparation: None is needed, although it is better not to book during a period because blood makes the sample harder to read, and vaginal medicines, lubricants and spermicides are avoided for a couple of days beforehand. A test that falls due in pregnancy is usually put off, and screening is normally taken up again about twelve weeks after giving birth; anyone who is pregnant and has been invited should say so when booking. Discomfort and anxiety can be reduced by asking for a smaller speculum, a different position or a longer appointment, and a course of vaginal oestrogen is sometimes prescribed first when the tissues are thin after the menopause or on testosterone.

interpretation.meaning: Routine recall; the chance of cervical cancer developing before the next invitation is very low
Screening is repeated in a year, because most infections clear on their own

interpretation.finding: High-risk HPV found with abnormal cells
interpretation.meaning: Referral for colposcopy: the cervix is examined under magnification and a biopsy or loop excision may be taken

interpretation.finding: High-risk HPV still present on repeat testing
interpretation.meaning: Screening is repeated after a further year; high-risk HPV that is still present at that second repeat leads to colposcopy even when the cells look normal, because it is persistent infection that leads to cancer
Repeated after about three months; repeated inadequate samples lead to colposcopy

cervical-screening.limitations: Screening lowers the risk of cervical cancer a great deal but does not remove it. HPV vaccination protects against the commonest high-risk types but not all of them, so screening invitations still apply to people who have been vaccinated. A sample can miss an abnormal area, and adenocarcinoma arising high in the cervical canal is harder to detect than squamous disease. A positive HPV result is common, says nothing about when or from whom the virus was acquired, and in most people clears without treatment within about two years. The test says nothing about the ovaries, the lining of the uterus or other infections, and it cannot be used to investigate bleeding or pain, which need an examination. Kits for taking a sample at home are being introduced in some programmes for people who do not attend.
